paper.title: Supervised prediction of drug-target interactions using bipartite local models
paper.citation: Bleakley K, Yamanishi Y. Supervised prediction of drug-target interactions using bipartite local models. Bioinformatics 25(18):2397-2403 (2009).

assumptions.what: A local model with no positive training example scores -1. The paper does not define this case; it covers 288 pairs for BLMd and 177 for BLMt on this dataset.
assumptions.sensitivity: Calibrated on the nuclear receptor dataset, where the rule changes BLMt AUC from 53.7 (-1) to 95.2 (score 0) and 91.5 (the pair left unscored) against the paper's 53.6, then used unchanged on the other three datasets.

assumptions.what: Scores are turned into z-scores before the maximum. The paper gives m(x, y) = max(x, y) and does not say whether it standardized first.
assumptions.sensitivity: Without standardizing, m(BLMd,BLMt) AUPR is 85.9 against the paper's 84.1 here and 84.2 against 77.9 on the ion channel dataset, and m(NNd,NNt) AUPR is 61.8 against 63.8; with it, 84.2, 78.1 and 63.8. The rule was chosen on all four datasets at once.

assumptions.what: The kernel regression solve is regularized by dropping singular values below 1e-2 of the largest. Neither this paper nor Yamanishi et al. (2008) gives a regularization, and the chemical similarity matrix is ill conditioned.
assumptions.sensitivity: On the GPCR dataset KRMd AUC is 64.8 unregularized, 84.6 at 1e-3, 86.8 at 1e-2 and 81.1 at 1e-1, against the paper's 87.3. KRMt, whose matrix is well conditioned, moves by less than 0.1 between 1e-15 and 1e-2.

assumptions.what: The area under the precision-recall curve joins the points with straight lines (the trapezoid rule). The paper says R was used but not how the area was taken.
assumptions.sensitivity: The step rule (average precision) moves the nearest-neighbour rows by up to 10 points (NNd 33.5 to 23.1 on the GPCR dataset) and the BLM rows by less than 1.

cause.summary: 11 of the 24 printed values come back to the digit and 21 are within one point. The largest gaps are the KRM AUPRs (KRMd 35.0 against 38.7, KRMt 78.3 against 80.6): the AUCs the paper stars for those rows are copied from Yamanishi et al. (2008), where they came from 10-fold cross-validation, so their leave-one-out AUPR cannot be checked against the same run. Three settings the paper does not give were identified against its own values and are listed as assumptions.

The pixel score sits near 50 per cent because two of the three curves are dashed and the phase of the dashes, which the PDF does not fix to the data, decides where ink falls inside a line.

items.label: Table 5, top 10 predicted nuclear receptor pairs

cause.summary: All ten pairs of the paper's Table 5 are in our top ten, and the five pairs of the Isotretinoin block come out in the paper's own order. Five sit at a different rank: our ranks 1 and 2 are the paper's 2 and 1, and its ranks 8, 9 and 10 are our 9, 10 and 8. Those five pairs are separated by at most 0.08 of a score unit, and the five Isotretinoin pairs are exactly tied at 0.194683 because they come from one local model, so their printed order is a tie break the paper does not state.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The pairs at a different rank are separated by less than the spread the undocumented settings cause.
hypotheses.test: The aggregated scores of the ten pairs, and the five tied Isotretinoin pairs.

cause.summary: The claim holds in our run, but none of its eight numbers is exact. The values it moves to come back as 84.2, 80.9, 66.6 and 60.0 against the printed 84.1, 81.3, 66.7 and 61.2, and the ones it moves from, the best KRM AUPRs, as 78.3, 76.9, 57.5 and 39.3 against 80.6, 79.6, 57.7 and 43.6. The gap is on the comparison method: its AUPR sits 2 to 4 points low on three datasets, while every BLM row is within a point. The rows whose AUC the paper took from Yamanishi et al. (2008) are the rows whose AUPR we cannot check against that paper, because it prints none.

items.label: Sections 4.1 to 4.3, how many of the eight conditions the local models win

cause.summary: Two of the three counts are one higher in our run: eight of eight conditions instead of seven in Section 4.1 and seven instead of six in Section 4.2. Both differences come from values that tie in the paper and separate here. The paper's seven of eight needs its ion channel AUC tie (KRMd and BLMd both 74.5) to count against the local models; our run gives 74.7 and 74.0, so the tie is gone. In Section 4.2 the paper's own tables give six only when the nearest-neighbour row is left out of the comparison, which is how this check reads it.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The counts are over the three method rows of each part, not over all four rows including the nearest-neighbour baseline.
hypotheses.test: Both readings against the paper's own tables (the arithmetic check in claims.py).

hypotheses.hypothesis: A tie between a KRM row and a BLM row counts as a win for the local models.
hypotheses.test: Both tie rules against the paper's own tables.

Sections 4.5 and 5, at least 4 of the top 10 nuclear receptor predictions were later confirmed

cause.summary: The confirmation status is a lookup in the SuperTarget database as of January 2009 and a literature search, not a computation. SuperTarget has been superseded and no January 2009 release is archived, so the status of the ten pairs cannot be recovered as the paper found it. Our run ranks the same ten pairs first, which is the part of the claim the method decides.

items.label: The authors' implementation against this one

cause.summary: The authors' MATLAB implementation is lost. The paper offers it on request and links a project page, which is now a redirect to the laboratory's home page; the Wayback Machine holds the page from 2014 and 2015, which lists bipartiteLocalModel.m and a data archive, but no capture of either file, and no copy is on GitHub. The method is therefore written from the paper's text and checked against its printed values.
